To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) decoupling data and computation scheduling can be beneficial in distributed data intensive systems; (2) the benefit is more pronounced in systems with high data transfer rates and high replication costs; and (3) the benefit is reduced as the data transfer rates decrease and the replication cost increases.

(1) data movement and computation can be decoupled, (2) data movement is best done asynchronously based on access patterns, and (3) the impact of replication is significant but can be handled without coupling data movement and computation.

(i) data movement and scheduling are not necessarily tied to each other, (ii) data movement is a function of data access pattern and load, and (iii) data movement can be performed asynchronously to scheduling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
scheduling and data movement in large scale data intensive environments.
the development of a scheduling framework that can be used in conjunction with a variety of data movement strategies.
the design and implementation of a scheduling framework that can be applied to a wide range of data grid applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best approach depends on the application.
the best solution is to decouple the computation scheduling from the data scheduling, but to use a data-aware scheduler that takes into account the data location information.
decoupled data movement can improve performance in many cases, and that the performance gain depends on the application, the data access pattern, and the scheduling policy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a scheduling framework that allows us to schedule data and jobs in a distributed data intensive application.
the decoupled approach performs as well as or better than the coupled approach, and it has the added benefit of simplifying implementation.
we are able to decouple computation and data scheduling and achieve better performance than the coupled approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the scheduling problem in Data Grids is more tractable when decoupling the data and computation scheduling decisions.
decoupling data movement and computation can significantly simplify the implementation of data intensive application scheduling, while still providing good performance.
the scheduling of data intensive applications can be decoupled from the movement of data.
